title: How Secrets Leak Through AI Agents (and How to Stop It) — Venice AI
talk_summary: A Venice AI developer-relations talk on privacy architecture for agentic systems, arguing that secrets should never enter the LLM reasoning layer and that observability logging, tool scope, and sandboxing are the main leak surfaces. It offers a few concrete architectural patterns (vault bound to the runtime not the model, narrow tool scope, classification layer) but is mostly vendor framing with no measured results.

takeaways.technique: Bind secret vault to the execution runtime, not the reasoning layer
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of the LLM reasoning layer fetching credentials from a vault and passing them into tool calls, they attach the vault to the deterministic agent runtime so the model only emits non-deterministic inputs and never sees the secret.
takeaways.evidence_quote: by tying the password vault to the agentic runtime instead of the reasoning layer ... the agent runtime is essentially turned into an execution layer

takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than exposing all 15-20 tools from an MCP server to an agent, grant only the one tool needed, so a compromised or confused agent has fewer exfiltration paths and a tighter context loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't really want to use all of them. You actually only really need one

takeaways.technique: Keep context window near-empty via narrow scope
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues that filling the context window degrades performance and that narrow tool scope keeps context small, improving agent output quality.
Put a pre-agent filter in front of the agent to detect prompt injection, implemented either as an LLM classifier, a vector-search semantic layer (Qdrant/LanceDB), or an in-memory process.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we also have a classification layer in front of an agent to check for prompt injection

takeaways.technique: Scrub observability logs of prompts and secrets
takeaways.what_they_do: Warns that default logging of prompts/traces can persist secrets and PII, and that this must be deliberately prevented rather than assumed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can also accidentally store prompts and secrets by default if you're not careful

takeaways.technique: Sandboxing is necessary but not sufficient
takeaways.what_they_do: Notes that VMs/sandboxes (Firecracker, EC2 in VPC) improve isolation but internet-enabled agents can still exfiltrate via external APIs, so permission monitoring is required.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have internet access enabled for your agent, it can still accidentally exfiltrate data through external API access
